Emotions & Feelings for 2-Year-Olds

Age 2 YearsSubject Talk & ConnectClass Toddler 7Duration 3–5 minutes

Happy, sad, angry, excited — little feelings can have big names. Look at the faces together and give those feelings simple words.

Nothing to read and nothing to fix. You name the feeling, your toddler makes the face — a point or a giggle counts. Stop whenever they have had enough.

TOGETHER · WHAT CAN WE DO?

What can we do?

No scripts needed. When feelings run big, one calm sentence is enough — a few to keep in your pocket.

  • Sad

    “Want a hug?”

  • Angry

    “Let’s slow down together.”

  • Scared

    “Stay close.”

  • Frustrated

    “Let’s try together.”

  • Tired

    “Maybe it’s time for a rest.”

SOLVE THE SHEETS — ON PAPER OR ON SCREEN

Solve the feelings cards together.

The twenty feeling cards print two to a page. On paper they become the best kind of feelings practice — naming a face, making the face, and finding your own.

  1. 01

    Print the cards

    Open the printable cards and print all twenty, two to a page. Cut them out together, naming each feeling as it is cut.

  2. 02

    Make the face

    Pick a card and make that face in a mirror together — happy, sad, silly, brave. The face teaches the word.

  3. 03

    Guess my feeling

    Make a feeling face and let your toddler find the matching card. Then swap: your child makes the face, you guess.

  4. 04

    Find today’s feeling

    Ask “how do you feel right now?” and lay that card on the table. One honest card, chosen freely, is the whole exercise.

TAKE IT OFF SCREEN

Feelings in our day.

Name feelings when they naturally come up today.

Try one today

  • “You’re smiling. You look happy!”
  • “That was frustrating.”
  • “You look tired.”
  • “Are you feeling excited?”
  • Make silly faces together in a mirror.

You name it and move on — no quizzing, no waiting for an answer. One feeling shared together is a complete class.

TIPS FOR PARENTS

Tips for Parents

All feelings are welcome here. Angry, sad and scared are not bad feelings — they are simply feelings, and every one of them has a name.

Go face first. Pull the expression yourself and your toddler will copy it — copying comes long before naming.

Name your own feelings too. “I’m happy you’re here” or “I’m tired tonight” — your face is the best flashcard in the house.

Age ranges are a guide. Go at your child’s pace.

    Happy — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson starts the feelings deck where every toddler already lives: happy. The card gives the grin a face to study, and the day supplies a hundred real moments to name it.

    What is this?

    Happy is the feeling that arrives with a grin, a bounce and a shout — the one your toddler produces daily without any help. The card puts a face on it so the word has somewhere to stick.

    What does it mean?

    Feelings are invisible until they get faces and words. Naming happy while it is happening builds the bridge between what a child feels inside and what everyone can see — the start of all self-knowledge.

    What does the child need to know?

    Any grin counts as an answer: a copied smile, a pointed finger, or happy shouted mid-giggle. Nothing is being tested — you are simply giving the good feeling its name, over and over, while it lasts.

    Why this matters

    Happy happens many times a day, free of charge. A feeling word with that many live rehearsals sticks fast — and once happy is named, every other feeling has a template to fit.

    What it teaches

    Feeling vocabulary, face-reading, and self-noticing — your toddler connecting their own inside weather to a word another person can understand.

    Words to learn

    happysmilefacegringladlaugh

    Say this to your child

    “"Happy! Look at this face — what a big smile. Can you do that happy face? There it is! You look happy right now. Happy, happy — the best feeling to say."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and name the feeling twice: happy — this face is feeling happy. Let your voice smile along with the word.
    2. Make the face together: pull your biggest grin, hold it, wobble it. A mirror doubles the fun if one is close.
    3. Catch happy live: next giggle, say it on the spot — you look happy! The word lands hardest in the very second the feeling is here.
    4. Accept every version: a grin, a point at the card, or a delighted happy! are all complete answers at two.
    5. Keep naming it all week — happy at the swing, happy at the snack, happy at the reunion — so the word attaches to the feeling, not to the card.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows an illustrated child having a happy feeling — one face, one feeling, nothing else competing. Ask your toddler to find the face, then make one just like it at their own face.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the happy face?" "Can you make that face?" "Who looks happy right now?" "Did you feel happy today?"

    What your child can say or do

    Expect happy delivered with the matching grin — a word worn on the face. Some toddlers answer by pointing at themselves, which is the self-noticing skill arriving early; some just giggle, and the giggle is an answer.

    Out in the real world

    Happy moments arrive all day without scheduling: the swing, the dog, the biscuit. Say the word at each one and the card keeps teaching from the drawer without being fetched.

    Try it together

    Happy hunt: make happy faces at each other across the table until someone laughs — then name what just happened. The laughter proves the feeling, and the naming proves the word.

    Understanding check

    Next time a big grin appears, ask how do you feel? A happy, a grin, or a bounce all pass. Then show the card at a flat moment — if your toddler still finds the happy face, the picture has become the dictionary.

    Parent tips

    Name the feeling while it is happening, not after: the live version sticks. Stay light — this card should never become a demand to perform happiness; it is a label for something already there.

    Staying safe

    No safety angle here — happy is the lowest-risk lesson in the deck. The only note: let the feeling be real, not commanded; toddlers cannot manufacture smiles on request, and nobody should have to.

    This lesson pairs with the Happy flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Emotions & Feelings (Toddler 7).

    Sad — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson introduces the down feeling with the same calm voice as all the others: sad gets a face on a card, a word that fits in a small mouth, and a grown-up who stays.

    What is this?

    Sad is the feeling that brings droopy shoulders, a wobbly lip and sometimes tears — the one that asks for company. The card shows it safely, where it can be looked at without living it.

    What does it mean?

    A named sadness is a smaller sadness: the word gives your toddler something to hold while the feeling passes. Being allowed to look at sad on a card teaches that this feeling is normal, welcome and survivable.

    What does the child need to know?

    Expect pointing, a quiet face, or a solemn word — sad is a soft answer, not a performance. If tears arrive during the lesson, the lesson has arrived in real life: comfort first, card later.

    Why this matters

    Small sorrows fill a toddler’s week — the dropped biscuit, the finished song, the door that closed. Each one is a live chance to say the word gently and mean it.

    What it teaches

    Feeling vocabulary for the hard feelings, comfort-seeking, and the deep lesson that all feelings are allowed — sad included, always.

    Words to learn

    sadtearscuddlefeelingssoftbetter

    Say this to your child

    “"Sad. This little face is feeling sad — see the soft eyes? Sometimes we all feel sad. If you feel sad, come and find me. Cuddles help. Sad goes away, and love stays."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card with a quiet voice: sad — this face is feeling sad. Let the calm in your voice do the first teaching.
    2. Make a sad face together in the mirror: droopy mouth, soft eyes. Two seconds is plenty — then let the faces rest.
    3. Ask where the sad face is and let your toddler find it; a gentle point is a full answer.
    4. When a real small sorrow shows up, name it low and slow: that made you sad. Then open your arms — the cuddle is part of the lesson, not a break from it.
    5. Return to the card afterwards, once the tears have dried: you felt sad, and now you feel better. The full arc, told in eight words.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows an illustrated child having a sad feeling — one quiet face to study. Ask your toddler to find the sad face, then to show you their own sad face, soft and slow.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the sad face?" "Can you do a sad face?" "What helps when you feel sad?" "Who gives good cuddles?"

    What your child can say or do

    A solemn point, a practiced droopy face, or sad whispered like a secret — all are answers. Some toddlers pat the card kindly; the comforting instinct is the deepest version of this lesson.

    Out in the real world

    Real sad moments are the lesson: name the feeling when it comes, stay close, and let the tears run their course. The card can wait on the shelf — the feeling cannot.

    Try it together

    Cuddle corner: when sadness visits, take your toddler and the card to a soft spot together. Look at the sad face, say the word once, and let the cuddle do the rest of the talking.

    Understanding check

    After a real sad moment has passed, show the card and ask what happened. A point, a sad face, or the word itself means the feeling and the label have met. Comfort given and received is the pass mark, every time.

    Parent tips

    Your calm is the whole atmosphere: sad named in a steady voice teaches that the feeling is survivable. Resist fixing fast — the sitting-with is the skill, and it is your skill as much as theirs.

    Staying safe

    Sad is allowed, always; tears are allowed too. The honest note: if sadness lingers for days, eats the appetite or the sleep, that is beyond a card — bring it to your health visitor or doctor, who are there for exactly this.

    This lesson pairs with the Sad flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Emotions & Feelings (Toddler 7).

    Angry — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson teaches angry on purpose, in a peaceful moment, long before the next storm: the face gets studied, the word gets practised, and the rule gets agreed while everyone is calm.

    What is this?

    Angry is the hot feeling — clenched fists, loud voice, a body that wants to explode. The card shows the face with no thunder attached, which is exactly why it works.

    What does it mean?

    Anger named in advance becomes survivable in the moment: a toddler who owns the word has a handrail while the feeling roars. The feeling is allowed; what the body does with it has rules.

    What does the child need to know?

    Play the card when everyone is calm, not mid-meltdown. In the storm, keep it to two words — you are angry — and save the rest for after, when the card and the story can meet again.

    Why this matters

    Anger visits every day at two: the block that fell, the shoe that lost, the biscuit that is gone. A word and a plan turn each storm from a catastrophe into weather.

    What it teaches

    Feeling vocabulary for big storms, body-awareness, and the first behaviour rule — all feelings are welcome, hurting is not.

    Words to learn

    angrycrossroarstompstormcalm

    Say this to your child

    “"Angry! This face is feeling angry — look at those eyebrows. Can you make an angry face? Grrr! When you feel angry, stomp and roar — and I will stay right here. All feelings are welcome; hurting is not."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card in a calm moment and name it strongly: angry — this face is feeling angry. Let the word sound big and safe at once.
    2. Make the face together: scrunch, frown, growl a little roar. The pretending gives the feeling a rehearsal room with no consequences.
    3. Give the storm its safe outlets, agreed in advance: stomp your feet, squeeze your fists, roar at the ceiling — angry is allowed to be loud.
    4. Say the rule plainly, while everyone is smiling: all feelings are welcome, and hurting is not. We stomp, we squeeze, we never hit.
    5. In the next real storm, keep it tiny: you are angry. Two words, then quiet company. Afterwards, return to the card and let the story be told.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows an illustrated child having an angry feeling — one stormy face, safely framed. Ask your toddler to find the angry face, then to show you their best pretend growl.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the angry face?" "Can you make that face?" "What can we do when we feel angry?" "Is hitting allowed?"

    What your child can say or do

    A stomping march around the rug, a growl at the ceiling, or angry barked at the card itself — all are the word doing its work. Some toddlers go quiet and point; the pointing counts exactly the same.

    Out in the real world

    Storms arrive on their own schedule. In the moment, the word plus your calm presence is the whole lesson; the card comes back out afterwards, when the retelling turns a meltdown into a story with an ending.

    Try it together

    Stomp-and-roar corner: when the thunder starts, walk together to one safe spot and let the angry body do its permitted thing — stomping, roaring, squeezing a cushion. Then the storm always ends, and you are still there.

    Understanding check

    After the next storm passes, show the card and ask what that feeling was. Angry, said or pointed, means the word is moving in. Feet that stomped and hands that stayed kind mean the rule landed too.

    Parent tips

    Keep yourself dull and steady through real storms — your steadiness is the teaching. Afterwards, retell it warmly: you were angry, you stomped, it passed. The story teaches more than the storm ever could.

    Staying safe

    The line every toddler needs spoken out loud: all feelings are welcome, hurting is never allowed. Storms get safe outlets — stomping, roaring, cushion-squeezing — and a grown-up who stays close without joining in.

    This lesson pairs with the Angry flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Emotions & Feelings (Toddler 7).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · EMOTIONS & FEELINGS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Scared — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson lets your toddler study fear from the safest seat there is: a card, a cuddle, and a word. Nobody here has to be brave — the feeling just gets to have a name.

    What is this?

    Scared is the wide-eyed feeling that arrives with loud noises, big dogs and dark corners — the one that sends small bodies behind trusted legs. The card shows it without any danger attached.

    What does it mean?

    A fear named is a fear that can be talked about: your toddler learns that scared is a feeling everyone has, and that saying it brings help instead of shame. Safety grows from company, not from pushing.

    What does the child need to know?

    Study the face, make it gently if your toddler wants to, and never demand bravery. If a real fright arrives, the order is fixed: feeling named, closeness given, story told afterwards.

    Why this matters

    Frights are daily at two — the hoover, the thunder, the hand-dryer. A word that works mid-scare turns each one into a moment of connection instead of chaos.

    What it teaches

    Feeling vocabulary for the wobbliest feeling, comfort-seeking, and the trust loop — fear named, grown-up arrives, world made safe again.

    Words to learn

    scaredhidecuddlesafebravehere

    Say this to your child

    “"Scared. This face is feeling scared — big wide eyes. Everyone feels scared sometimes. When you feel scared, say scared, and I will come. I stay close. The scared feeling gets smaller with company."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card softly: scared — this face is feeling scared. Wide eyes, tucked-in arms. Let your toddler look as long as they like.
    2. Make the face together, briefly and kindly: wide eyes, small squeak. Then let the faces rest — pretending is a game, not an exam.
    3. Say the ending every story needs: when you feel scared, I come to you, and we stay close until the scared feeling goes.
    4. If a real fright happens, name it in one breath — that noise gave you a scare — then scoop, settle, stay. The card can join in afterwards.
    5. Retell the fright gently once it is over: the noise happened, you felt scared, I came, and then it was fine. Stories with endings shrink fears.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows an illustrated child having a scared feeling — one wide-eyed face to study from a safe distance. Ask your toddler to find the scared face, and to point at what the arms are doing.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the scared face?" "Can you make a scared face?" "What helps when you feel scared?" "Who comes when you call?"

    What your child can say or do

    A point from a safe lap, a whispered scared, or hiding the card behind a cushion — all are answers, and the hiding is honest too. Some toddlers simply lean into you; leaning is the lesson working.

    Out in the real world

    Real frights get the same script every time: name the feeling, offer the closeness, add the ending later. Your toddler learns the sequence by heart — feeling, word, grown-up, calm.

    Try it together

    Brave-and-safe game: hide a toy somewhere mild, find it together, and narrate — the toy felt scared, then you came, now it is happy. Your toddler gets to be the rescuer, which is the deepest way to learn the script.

    Understanding check

    After the next fright, ask later: what did you feel? A scared, a point at the card, or hiding behind your leg with eye contact all pass. The real pass mark is the arm that reaches for you — trust installed.

    Parent tips

    Take fears at face value and answer them with company, not logic. Skip teasing entirely — a mocked fear teaches hiding, not courage. Your calm is the shelter; the word is the door into it.

    Staying safe

    All feelings are welcome, and scared most of all needs saying out loud. Never push a frightened child toward the scary thing — closeness first, retreat freely offered, and progress at the pace of the child.

    This lesson pairs with the Scared flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Emotions & Feelings (Toddler 7).

    Surprised — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson turns the deck’s funniest face into a game: surprise, manufactured gently at home, named out loud the instant the eyebrows shoot up.

    What is this?

    Surprised is the sudden feeling — eyebrows high, mouth open, a gasp before the laugh. It arrives when the world does something unexpected, and toddlers meet it daily: peek-a-boo, pop-up toys, disappearing biscuits.

    What does it mean?

    Surprise is the friendly edge of the big feelings: it startles without hurting, and it teaches that feelings arrive suddenly and pass quickly. It is also the gateway card — once the face game is fun, the heavier faces feel lighter.

    What does the child need to know?

    The gasp is the answer: a surprised oh!, a squeal, or both eyebrows climbing are complete. Manufacture the feeling small and kind — gentle reveals, never jumps — and name it while the eyebrows are still up.

    Why this matters

    Surprise hides inside the games toddlers already play: covered cups, pop-up books, socks that turn out to be on hands. Every reveal is a rehearsal with the word attached.

    What it teaches

    Feeling vocabulary, sudden-change tolerance, and face-reading — plus the comedy timing that makes toddlers the best audiences on earth.

    Words to learn

    surprisedwowohpeekpopgasp

    Say this to your child

    “"Surprised! Oh — look at that face! Eyebrows up, mouth open: ohh! Watch the cup… one, two… pop! Surprised! Can you do the surprised face? Now you hide the toy and surprise me!"”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card with drama: surprised — look at those eyebrows! Let your own eyebrows join in from the first word.
    2. Make the face together: hands on cheeks, mouth open, a big ohh! Practise it twice, then keep it in your pockets for later.
    3. Play a gentle reveal: hide a toy under a tea towel, count to two, whisk it off and gasp surprised! together. Repeat until the giggles take over.
    4. Name real surprises live: the toast pops, the dog barks, the bubble pops — surprised! The word should chase the feeling by half a second.
    5. Let your toddler run the reveal: their turn to cover, count and lift, while you do the gasping. Being the surpriser teaches the timing from the inside.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows an illustrated child having a surprised feeling — one open-mouthed face, eyebrows high. Ask your toddler to find the surprised face, then to point at the mouth and the eyebrows that tell the story.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the surprised face?" "Can you make that face?" "What happened — pop! How do you feel?" "Whose turn to surprise?"

    What your child can say or do

    A gasp, a squeal, or surprised delivered as a delighted brrrp! — the face will arrive long before the word does. Some toddlers stage the whole reveal themselves and gasp on your behalf; that is directing, and it counts.

    Out in the real world

    Surprises pepper the day without any planning: the kettle clicks, the light goes on, a friend appears. Catch two a day with the word and the feeling owns its name by Friday.

    Try it together

    Peek-cup theatre: three cups, one toy, slow reveals with big gasps. Let your toddler swap which cup hides the toy while your back is turned — being surprised well is a gift you give them.

    Understanding check

    Next gentle surprise, watch the face: eyebrows up means the feeling arrived, and a surprised or an ohh means the word rode along. Then ask later where the surprised face is — a quick find closes the loop.

    Parent tips

    Keep every manufactured surprise kind and slow — this game lives next door to startle, and startle is not the lesson. If your toddler dislikes surprises, study the face on the card and skip the reveals; the word still lands.

    Staying safe

    Surprises stay small and voluntary: no jump-scares, no hiding out of sight, no loud bangs — a startled toddler is a frightened one, and the difference matters. Reveal, gasp, giggle, repeat.

    This lesson pairs with the Surprised flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Emotions & Feelings (Toddler 7).

    Excited — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson names the feeling your toddler wears most afternoons: the pre-park wiggles, the pre-birthday bounce. Excited gets a face on a card and a permission slip for the noise.

    What is this?

    Excited is the can’t-sit-still feeling — bouncing, squealing, talking fast, wanting the good thing to start now. The card shows it as a face; your toddler shows it as weather.

    What does it mean?

    Named excitement sometimes settles by itself: a body that hears you are so excited! often wobbles a little slower, because the feeling has been seen. Naming is not a cure-all — it is a hand on the shoulder.

    What does the child need to know?

    The feeling is allowed, loudly. The behaviour has banks to run between: bouncing yes, bouncing off the sofa no. Expect excited, a wiggle-demo, or a squeal as answers — all three pass.

    Why this matters

    Excitement precedes most of the best moments of toddler life, which makes this the highest-frequency feeling in the deck. The word gets daily rehearsals for free.

    What it teaches

    Feeling vocabulary for high energy, body-awareness, and the first hint that naming a feeling helps steer it — emotional literacy in its native habitat.

    Words to learn

    excitedwigglebouncewowreadybig

    Say this to your child

    “"Excited! Look at this face — so wiggly! Are you excited? Bounce like this — wiggle, wiggle, wiggle! Excited is a big, loud feeling and it is allowed. And when we get there… wow."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and name it with energy: excited — this face cannot sit still! Let your own body wiggle the word.
    2. Make the face and the wiggle together: wide eyes, bouncing shoulders, hands a-flutter. Two wiggly seconds, then settle.
    3. Catch the real thing live: before the park, before dinner guests, before anything good — you are excited! The word arrives while the wiggles are at their best.
    4. Give the feeling its safe channels: bounce on the spot, wiggle like jelly, squeeze-and-release. Excited bodies get to move — just not off furniture.
    5. After the good thing happens, retell it: you were so excited, and then — the park! The word and the memory file together.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows an illustrated child having an excited feeling — one wide-awake face full of energy. Ask your toddler to find the excited face, then to show you their own wiggle.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the excited face?" "Can you wiggle like that?" "Are you excited right now?" "What is coming that is good?"

    What your child can say or do

    A bounce that says the word for them, a squealed excited!, or both hands waving — the body is the main speaker here. Some toddlers freeze mid-wiggle when named, surprised to be seen; the freeze is the word landing.

    Out in the real world

    Excitement announces itself daily: shoes by the door, the kettle for bath time, a friend at the window. Name it before the event, and the word becomes part of the anticipation — which is half the fun.

    Try it together

    Wiggle stop-dance: excited music on, everyone wiggles; music off, everyone freezes. The freeze is the skill — a body that can go from full bounce to still is a body learning its own volume dial.

    Understanding check

    Before the next good thing, ask how do you feel? An excited, a bounce, or a wiggly nod all pass. Then watch for the word appearing unprompted in your toddler’s own mouth — that is the graduation.

    Parent tips

    Say the feeling instead of calm down, which has never once worked in the history of toddlers. Naming first, wiggle-channel second, expectation third: excitement managed is excitement enjoyed.

    Staying safe

    The feeling is always allowed; the body has banks to stay within — no bouncing on sofas, no sprinting toward roads, no wiggling at the top of the stairs. Give the energy a floor, and it gives you a show.

    This lesson pairs with the Excited flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Emotions & Feelings (Toddler 7).

    Tired — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson teaches the feeling that arrives every evening whether anyone invites it or not: tired. The card gives the droop a face, and the wind-down gives it a routine.

    What is this?

    Tired is the end-of-day feeling — heavy eyelids, slow body, short temper. Toddlers show it constantly and fight it constantly, which is exactly why the word is worth its weight in calm.

    What does it mean?

    A named tired feeling can be surrendered to: your body is tired, it is asking for rest works on a toddler in a way bedtime does not. The word turns rest from a punishment into an answer.

    What does the child need to know?

    Expect a yawn, a droopy demonstration, or a tired whispered from under a fringe. Name the feeling early — before the storm — and let the routine carry the rest.

    Why this matters

    Tired visits daily, usually on schedule, and it sits behind a fair share of afternoon meltdowns. A word for it is a fire extinguisher mounted by the door.

    What it teaches

    Feeling vocabulary for body signals, self-noticing, and the habit of reading your own body — the earliest form of self-care.

    Words to learn

    tiredsleepyrestyawnbedquiet

    Say this to your child

    “"Tired. This face is feeling tired — sleepy eyes, big yawn. Is your body tired? Tired means time for rest. Come here, let us be quiet together. Sleep is coming, and that is good."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card at a quiet moment: tired — this face is feeling tired. Let your voice drop low, because tired words travel best softly.
    2. Make the face together: droopy eyes, a big theatrical yawn, shoulders sliding down. The pretending is gentle comedy and it lands.
    3. Name the real thing early in the evening: your body feels tired — look, the tired face! Say it before the tears, not after.
    4. Connect the word to the routine: tired means rest — pyjamas, book, bed. The feeling has a plan, and the plan is kind.
    5. In the morning, close the loop: you were tired, you slept, and now look at you. The arc teaches that tired always has an answer.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows an illustrated child having a tired feeling — one droopy, sleepy face. Ask your toddler to find the tired face, then to make their very best yawn next to it.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the tired face?" "Can you yawn like that?" "Is your body tired?" "What does tired mean it is time for?"

    What your child can say or do

    A yawn caught and copied, a droopy slide to the floor, or tired murmured from inside a cuddle — all are answers. Some toddlers point at the card and then at themselves; that pointing is self-knowledge arriving.

    Out in the real world

    Tired shows up on time every evening and mid-morning after big outings. Name it at the first yawn and the word becomes the beginning of the wind-down instead of the middle of a fight.

    Try it together

    Big-yawn theatre: take turns doing the hugest, silliest yawns together, then let the silliness deflate into quiet. The game ends the way the feeling ends — soft, slow, and ready for blankets.

    Understanding check

    At the first evening yawn, ask how does your body feel? A tired, a yawn, or a lean into your shoulder all pass. A toddler who says tired and walks toward the cot has taken the whole lesson home.

    Parent tips

    Name tired before the wobbles start — the word works best at the first yawn, worst at the third meltdown. Pair it with the same routine every night; the feeling and the ritual learn each other.

    Staying safe

    Tired toddlers fall off things: the climbing urge and the droopy body are a bad mix, so low-energy play only after the word is said. Car-seat battles and tired bodies need extra patience and all the straps, every time.

    This lesson pairs with the Tired flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Emotions & Feelings (Toddler 7).
