    Calm — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson practises the deck’s quietest face while nobody needs it: calm, rehearsed in soft moments so it can be found again in loud ones. Two breaths at a time — that is the whole method.

    What is this?

    Calm is the settled feeling — slow breath, easy face, a body that is not in a hurry. The card shows it as a face; your toddler can feel it in two slow breaths, right on cue.

    What does it mean?

    Calm is the first feeling toddlers can switch on deliberately: breath is the one dial a two-year-old can actually turn. Practised daily, the slow breath becomes a tool the body owns before the words do.

    What does the child need to know?

    Expect a copy-cat breath, a soft sigh, or a solemn point — all are answers. Teach calm when everyone is already calm; asking for it mid-storm is like fishing in an empty bath.

    Why this matters

    Every storm needs a harbour. The calm face, practised in peace, becomes the picture your toddler’s body remembers when the next big feeling blows through.

    What it teaches

    Breath control, self-regulation in embryo, and quiet-time habits — the skill that turns every later meltdown shorter and every bedtime softer.

    Words to learn

    calmbreathslowquietsoftstill

    Say this to your child

    “"Calm. This face is feeling calm — see the soft eyes? Let us breathe like the calm face: smell the flower… and blow the feather. Quiet body, slow breath. This is calm. Lovely."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card in a soft voice: calm — this face is feeling calm. Let the word itself arrive slowly.
    2. Breathe together: sniff an imaginary flower — breathe in slow — and waft a feather — breathe out long. Two rounds is plenty; five gets silly.
    3. Make the calm face in a mirror: loose shoulders, easy mouth, sleepy-blinking eyes. Let your toddler study their own quiet face.
    4. Play a quiet game — rocking a toy to sleep, listening for the fridge hum — and name the feeling during it: this is calm. We are being calm right now.
    5. Practise at odd, peaceful moments all week: after the bath, in the buggy, before the story. The rehearsed feeling becomes findable on demand.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows an illustrated child having a calm feeling — one settled, easy face. Ask your toddler to find the calm face, then to make their own face soft and slow beside it.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the calm face?" "Can you make your face calm?" "Can you smell the flower with me?" "What do we do with a slow breath?"

    What your child can say or do

    A copy-cat breath with a wobbly exhale, a sigh from the belly, or a body that suddenly settles — the body speaks first here. Some toddlers shush you gently; being calm together is the whole exercise.

    Out in the real world

    Calm moments hide in the day: the buggy ride, the bath, the last story. Say the word during two of them and the feeling gets a daily home — ready for the day it is needed as a rescue.

    Try it together

    Flower-and-feather: sniff an imaginary bloom (slow in), waft a feather off your palm (slow out). Do it side by side, then let your toddler lead. Two breaths, three times a day, builds a regulator.

    Understanding check

    At the next small wobble, offer the breath: shall we smell the flower? A breath attempt, a settling body, or a point at the calm card all pass. Bodies that find calm faster than last week are the real report card.

    Parent tips

    Rehearse in peace or not at all — calm demanded mid-meltdown collapses. Keep your own breath slow and visible while you teach; toddlers borrow the nervous systems of the people they love.

    Staying safe

    Breathing games are the safest card in the deck; the honest note is about expectations — calm is a practice, not a switch, and storms still happen. Never use it as a punishment or a command to feel differently.

    This lesson pairs with the Calm flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Emotions & Feelings (Toddler 7).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · EMOTIONS & FEELINGS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Shy — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson gives a word to the feeling every toddler knows from birthday parties: shy. The card makes it studyable, and the plan makes it normal — new people take a minute.

    What is this?

    Shy is the hold-back feeling — watching from a distance, quiet voice, wanting to join from behind a trusted knee. The card shows it gently, as a feeling that visits everyone sometimes.

    What does it mean?

    Shyness named loses its sting: your toddler learns that taking a minute is a way of joining, not a failure to join. Warm-up time is how confidence is actually built — slowly, on the child’s own clock.

    What does the child need to know?

    Expect a point, a whisper, or a practiced hiding face — all answers. The lesson is permission: hello can wait, watching counts as taking part, and the minute belongs to the child.

    Why this matters

    New people appear weekly — the plumber, the new cousin, the other toddler at the gate. A word and a plan for the pause turns each arrival from a test into a process.

    What it teaches

    Feeling vocabulary for the quiet feelings, social warm-up, and self-advocacy in seed form — the right to take your time, learned early.

    Words to learn

    shyquietwatchhellominutewarm

    Say this to your child

    “"Shy. This face is feeling shy — peeking out, being quiet. It is okay to feel shy. New people take a minute. You can watch, you can wave, or you can say hello — whenever you are ready. I am right here."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card quietly: shy — this face is feeling a bit shy. Keep your voice close and small, like the feeling itself.
    2. Make the face together: peek out from behind your hands. The hiding can be a game — peek-a-shy — with a smile waiting at the end.
    3. Say the plan out loud: when new people come, you can say hello, or wave, or watch from my knee. All of it counts.
    4. At the next real arrival, name it softly if needed: feeling a bit shy? That is okay. Then stand nearby and do nothing else — the minute is doing the work.
    5. Afterwards, close gently: you watched for a while, and then you waved. The story teaches that warm-ups have happy endings.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows an illustrated child having a shy feeling — one quiet, peeking face. Ask your toddler to find the shy face, then to peek out from behind their own hands just like it.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the shy face?" "Can you peek out like that?" "What can we do when we feel shy?" "Are you ready to wave yet?"

    What your child can say or do

    A face half-hidden behind your leg, a whispered shy, or a slow emerging smile — all are the feeling speaking. A first tiny wave after minutes of watching is the milestone; nobody claps louder than they want.

    Out in the real world

    Every new face is a rehearsal: name the feeling only if your toddler wants it named, stand close, and let the warm-up run. The world becomes a place where shy has a script and an ending.

    Try it together

    Peek-a-shy at home: hide behind a door, a curtain, a teddy — and peek out with a slow smile. The game teaches that hiding and joining are neighbours, and the door between them opens from the child’s side.

    Understanding check

    After the next warm-up, ask how you felt at first. A shy, a point at the card, or a hiding grin all pass. Then watch what came after — a wave, a hello, a joined game — and name that part too.

    Parent tips

    Take the performance pressure off entirely: hello is an offer, not a duty. Skip apologies to strangers for a shy toddler; a calm this is how they take a minute respects the child and ends the moment.

    Staying safe

    All feelings welcome — including the quiet ones, which need it most. A shy child is never pushed forward to perform: no forced hellos, no handed-over-to-strangers, no making shyness into a show for grown-ups.

    This lesson pairs with the Shy flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Emotions & Feelings (Toddler 7).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · EMOTIONS & FEELINGS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Silly — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson names the feeling behind the fart jokes and the walking-backwards: silly. The card gives the giggles a face, and the day gets a sanctioned time and place for pure nonsense.

    What is this?

    Silly is the playful feeling — tongue out, googly eyes, a body that has decided everything is funny. The card shows it as a face; your toddler has been demonstrating it for months.

    What does it mean?

    Naming silly hands your toddler a word for deliberate play — the feeling they produce on purpose to make things fun. A feeling with a name can be requested, scheduled and shared, which is comedy in embryo.

    What does the child need to know?

    Expect an instant face, a giggle, or silly! shouted at full volume. The word lands fast because the feeling needs no introduction — your only job is the name and the venue.

    Why this matters

    Silly is the deck’s release valve: ten seconds of deliberate nonsense can reset an afternoon. A named, scheduled silly beats a chaotic one every time.

    What it teaches

    Humour development, deliberate play, and emotional vocabulary for joy — plus the social skill of reading when silliness is welcome.

    Words to learn

    sillyfunnyfacegigglegoofyjoke

    Say this to your child

    “"Silly! Look at this face — what a silly face! Can you make one? Tongue out… googly eyes… oh no, TOO silly! Silly is for playtime. Silly makes us laugh — your turn to be silly now."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and meet it with a grin: silly — this face is being so silly. Let your eyebrows start the game.
    2. Pull silly faces together: tongue out, puffed cheeks, crossed eyes. A mirror makes it a tournament; keep the rounds short.
    3. Name the feeling while the giggles run: you are being so silly! The word attaches itself — no drilling required.
    4. Give silly its frame: silly time lives in play, not at the dinner table or the shop checkout. Say the frame once, kindly, and hold it.
    5. Let your toddler run a round: they make the face, you do the laughing. The comedian-audience swap is the social half of the lesson.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows an illustrated child having a silly feeling — one tongue-out, playful face. Ask your toddler to find the silly face, then to make their silliest face right back at it.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the silly face?" "Can you do a silly face?" "Who is being silly right now?" "When is silly time?"

    What your child can say or do

    An instant tongue, a cross-eyed stare, or silly! barked like a command — the feeling arrives faster than any other card in the deck. Expect to be commanded to look; the audience is part of the game.

    Out in the real world

    Silly breaks out everywhere: the bath, the buggy, the wrong-hat game. Name it when it comes, enjoy it, and let the frame do the steering — silly named is silly shared.

    Try it together

    Silly-face tournament: two players, one mirror, faces escalate until someone laughs. Everyone loses, everyone wins — then a deep breath ends the tournament, and the silliness folds back into the afternoon.

    Understanding check

    Ask at a calm moment: show me the silly face. An instant tongue-out is a pass with honours. Then watch the frame: a toddler who saves the silliest material for playtime has learned the whole lesson, frame included.

    Parent tips

    Join in fully — silly is the one feeling that dies without an audience. Keep the frame firm and cheerful: silly has a time, and grown-ups will say when it is. That boundary is what makes the game last.

    Staying safe

    Silly bodies bump into things: the tournament stays on soft floors, away from furniture corners and stairs. The honest note — silliness can tip into wildness fast, and the grown-up owns the timer, not the toddler.

    This lesson pairs with the Silly flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Emotions & Feelings (Toddler 7).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · EMOTIONS & FEELINGS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Proud — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson catches the feeling that arrives just after a hard thing works: proud. The card gives the chin-up moment a face, and your words give it a name that makes the glow last.

    What is this?

    Proud is the earned feeling — chest out, chin up, a smile that cannot sit still, arriving after something took real trying. The card shows it as a face; your toddler supplies the achievements.

    What does it mean?

    Proud connects effort to feeling: your toddler learns that the warm glow after trying hard has a name, and that the name comes from inside them, not from a prize. That is the seed of healthy motivation.

    What does the child need to know?

    Name it at the moment of success and again at retelling: you did it — you look proud! Expect a grin, a cheer, or proud said with the chest puffed. All pass; the grin most of all.

    Why this matters

    Toddlers achieve hard things hourly — stairs, zips, towers. Each achievement is a live chance to wire effort to feeling, and the wiring is free.

    What it teaches

    Achievement vocabulary, effort-praise habits, and self-esteem built on doing — the feeling that makes toddlers try again tomorrow.

    Words to learn

    prouddidtryagainwowhard

    Say this to your child

    “"Proud! This face did something hard — look how it stands up tall! Can you stand like that? You did it! You kept trying and it worked. You must feel so proud. I am proud of you too."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and name the feeling: proud — this face did something hard and it worked! Let your chin lift as you say it.
    2. Make the face together: chest out, chin up, hands on hips. Superhero posture is the honest body language of this feeling.
    3. Catch it live: next tower, next zip, next step climbed — you did it! You look proud! The word lands while the glow is warm.
    4. Praise the trying out loud: you kept going, you tried again, you did it yourself. The effort is the story, not just the win.
    5. Retell it at bedtime: today you were proud, because you built the tower all by yourself. Named achievements become part of who your toddler is.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows an illustrated child having a proud feeling — one tall-standing, chin-up face. Ask your toddler to find the proud face, then to stand tall like it, hands on hips.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the proud face?" "Can you stand tall like that?" "What did you do today?" "How did it feel when it worked?"

    What your child can say or do

    A chest-out march, a both-arms-up did it!, or proud delivered as poud with full posture — the body carries the word. Some toddlers point at the card and then at their own tower; that pointing is the connection.

    Out in the real world

    Achievements fill the day: the shoe that went on, the cup that got carried, the step that got jumped. One named proud per day keeps the word warm and the trying coming.

    Try it together

    Did-it parade: at the end of the day, march through three things your toddler did themselves, each with a proud-face salute. The parade teaches the feeling by collecting the evidence.

    Understanding check

    After the next hard-won success, ask how do you feel? A proud, a chest-out grin, or a did it! all pass. Then listen for the word arriving unprompted in your toddler’s own retelling — that is the word moving in.

    Parent tips

    Praise the effort rather than the talent: words about keeping on build persistence, while clever-child talk quietly builds a fear of failing. Keep the word for genuine effort — your toddler’s own measure of hard is the one that counts.

    Staying safe

    No safety angle beyond cheering safely — the proud parade stays off the furniture. The honest note: let the child do the doing; help offered too fast steals the feeling this card exists to name.

    This lesson pairs with the Proud flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Emotions & Feelings (Toddler 7).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · EMOTIONS & FEELINGS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Worried — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson names the quiet, frowny feeling that comes before: a large dog, the strange cot, the first day somewhere new. Worried gets a word, and the word gets a plan.

    What is this?

    Worried is the before-feeling — furrowed brow, clingy body, questions in the eyes. It arrives when something might happen, and at two, most might-happens loom large.

    What does it mean?

    Worries shrink when they meet a plan: first shoes, then hello, then home. A plain map of what comes next gives the feeling edges — and your calm does the rest of the reassuring.

    What does the child need to know?

    Expect a point, a frown-copy, or worried said small. Do not argue the worry away or promise outcomes; acknowledge it, sketch the plan, and stand close. Company is the cure that works.

    Why this matters

    New things arrive weekly at two, and each one casts a shadow before it arrives. A named feeling with a named plan turns dread into a map your toddler can read.

    What it teaches

    Feeling vocabulary for anticipation, plan-making, and the trust loop — worry spoken, grown-up steady, world predictable again.

    Words to learn

    worriedhmmplannexttogetherhere

    Say this to your child

    “"Worried. This face is feeling worried — see the little frown? Everyone feels worried sometimes. When you do, tell me, and we will make a plan together. First this, then that — and I stay with you."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card gently: worried — this face is thinking about something that might happen. Furrowed brow and all.
    2. Make the face together, softly: small frown, chewing lip. Then let the face rest — the pretending stays light.
    3. Teach the tool: when you feel worried, we say worried, and then we make a plan. Plans make big feelings smaller.
    4. Rehearse on a small real one: the big dog tomorrow — first we look from the window, then we hold hands, then we decide. Say the plan in three beats.
    5. When a real worry visits, use the sequence: name it, plan it, stay close. Afterwards, tell how it went — the ending is the medicine.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows an illustrated child having a worried feeling — one furrowed, thinking face. Ask your toddler to find the worried face, then to make their own small thinking-frown beside it.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the worried face?" "Can you make a worried face?" "What helps when you feel worried?" "What is our plan?"

    What your child can say or do

    A point at the card, a worried whispered into your shoulder, or a frown offered in miniature — all are answers. A toddler who brings the card during a wobbly moment has learned to ask for help with it.

    Out in the real world

    Worries announce themselves in clingy days and stalling bedtimes. Name the feeling, sketch the next three steps out loud, and let your steadiness answer the part words cannot.

    Try it together

    Plan-the-day game: line up three toys and give the day a map — first blocks, then snack, then park. Toddlers who can see the shape of what happens next carry fewer unnamed worries.

    Understanding check

    After the next mapped event, ask how you felt before. A worried, a nod, or a point at the card all pass. The deeper pass mark: your toddler brings you the worry earlier next time — trust compounding.

    Parent tips

    Acknowledge before you reassure — yes, that dog is big comes first; the plan comes second. Skip promises about what will happen; your calm and the map together are the honest comfort.

    Staying safe

    All feelings welcome — including the pre-feelings that arrive early. Do not dismiss or mock a worry; acknowledge it and stay near. If worries grow big enough to run the day, a chat with your health visitor is the strong move, not a failure.

    This lesson pairs with the Worried flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Emotions & Feelings (Toddler 7).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · EMOTIONS & FEELINGS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Frustrated — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson names the feeling behind the block tower that fell again and the zip that will not budge: frustrated. The card hands the everyday tussle a face and a respectable name.

    What is this?

    Frustrated is the stuck feeling — gritted teeth, hot face, hands that want to throw. It visits when trying hard is not yet working, which at two is approximately hourly.

    What does it mean?

    The word works like a small reservoir of patience: naming the feeling gives the storm a shape, and a shaped feeling is easier to sit inside. Frustration survived is where persistence is actually built.

    What does the child need to know?

    Offer two exits when it strikes: asking for help, or one more go. Either exit begins with the feeling named — that is frustrating — and the throwing of toys gets its gentle limit.

    Why this matters

    Frustration is constant at two: cups that spill, lids that stick, towers that fall. A word this busy pays for itself before the week is out.

    What it teaches

    Persistence, feeling vocabulary for the struggle-zone, and choice-making — plus the deep lesson that hard feelings have words and exits.

    Words to learn

    frustratedhardhelptrystuckagain

    Say this to your child

    “"Frustrated! This face is trying so hard — and it still will not work. Grrr! That is frustrating. You can say help, or you can try again. I am here either way. Hard things get easier with trying."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and name it clearly: frustrated — this face is trying and trying and it will not work! Gritted teeth and all.
    2. Make the face together: clenched jaw, squeezed fists, a small grrr. The pretending gives the feeling a dress rehearsal.
    3. Teach the two doors: when you feel frustrated, you can say help please — or try again. Both doors are always open.
    4. At the next real struggle, lead with the word — so frustrating! The tower fell again. Then offer the two doors and wait one beat longer than feels comfortable.
    5. Afterward, retell the survival: it was frustrating, you tried again, and look — it worked. Or: I helped, and together we did it. Both endings count.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows an illustrated child having a frustrated feeling — one gritted, working-hard face. Ask your toddler to find the frustrated face, then to make their own grrr face, fists and all.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the frustrated face?" "Can you make a grrr face?" "What are our two choices when we feel frustrated?" "Do you want help or try again?"

    What your child can say or do

    A grrr with real feeling, help said as hep, or a determined second attempt with no words at all — all are the lesson working. A thrown cup means the feeling outran the word; name it, reset gently, keep the doors open.

    Out in the real world

    Struggles arrive all day: socks, lids, zips, puzzles. Name the feeling at the first grrr, offer the doors, and let the surviving do the teaching — frustration endured with company is persistence under construction.

    Try it together

    Stuck-point play: give your toddler a puzzle one step past easy, and stay close without fixing. When the grrr comes, offer the two doors and watch which one gets picked — then pick the other one yourself next time.

    Understanding check

    At the next struggle, listen for the word: frustrated, hep, or a look at the card mid-grrr all pass. Then watch the second attempt — a toddler who tries once more is building the muscle this card exists for.

    Parent tips

    Put the word in ahead of the solutions — the vocabulary is the bucket, the doors come second. Hold back one beat longer than instinct suggests; the gap between stuck and helped is where persistence grows.

    Staying safe

    All feelings welcome, and frustration is the most frequent guest. The limit stands beside it: throwing and hitting are not on the menu — stomping, squeezing and the two doors are. Move breakables; keep the toddler.

    This lesson pairs with the Frustrated flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Emotions & Feelings (Toddler 7).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · EMOTIONS & FEELINGS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Confused — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson names the face your toddler makes when routines bend: confused. The card gives the puzzlement a word, and slowing down gives it a way out.

    What is this?

    Confused is the what-is-happening feeling — tilted head, searching eyes, a pause mid-action. It arrives when the usual stops being usual: a different cup, a changed plan, a rule with edges nobody explained.

    What does it mean?

    Confusion is what learning looks like from the inside: the mind holds two versions of the world and hunts for the edit. Named calmly, it becomes interesting instead of alarming — what instead of wail.

    What does the child need to know?

    Expect a head-tilt copy, a puzzled hmm, or a point between two options — all answers. When it happens live, drop to slow motion and give the moment words; the fog clears at walking pace, never at a run.

    Why this matters

    The world changes its mind daily at two — the shop is shut, the cup is a new cup, Daddy wears a hat. A word for the in-between feeling keeps those moments curious instead of frightening.

    What it teaches

    Feeling vocabulary for the puzzlement-zone, flexibility when routines bend, and thinking out loud with a grown-up — cognitive skills with an emotional handle.

    Words to learn

    confusedhmmwhylooktogetherslow

    Say this to your child

    “"Confused. This face is thinking — hmm? What is happening? Everyone feels confused sometimes. When you do, we slow down and look together. Hmm… now we know! Confused always has an ending."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and name it with a raised eyebrow: confused — this face is thinking, hmm, what is happening here?
    2. Make the face together: tilted head, small frown, a questioning hmm. The copy is easy and funny — let the mirror judge.
    3. Teach the exit: when you feel confused, we slow down and look together. Say the sequence twice so it settles.
    4. When a real puzzler arrives — the cup is different, the plan has changed — narrate slowly: hmm, this is confusing! Come and look with me. Then actually look, at toddler pace.
    5. Close every puzzling moment with the resolution: now we know! The arc from confused to understood is the lesson, repeated in miniature all week.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows an illustrated child having a confused feeling — one tilted, puzzled face. Ask your toddler to find the confused face, then to make their own wondering hmm-face beside it.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the confused face?" "Can you make a hmm face?" "What do we do when we feel confused?" "What happened here?"

    What your child can say or do

    A tilted head, an honest hmm, or a finger pointing between two things — all are the feeling on display. Some toddlers hand you the confusing object directly; delegation is a perfectly good strategy.

    Out in the real world

    Puzzling moments appear without warning: the new cup, the closed park, the haircut. Name the feeling, slow the moment, look together — and the day’s surprises become problems the two of you solve.

    Try it together

    Mystery object: pop a household thing in a sock and let your toddler feel, frown and guess. The confused face is the point of the game — celebrate the hmm as loudly as the answer.

    Understanding check

    At the next puzzling change, watch for the tilt or listen for the hmm — either passes. Then ask later where the confused face is: a quick find plus a remembered hmm means the word and the feeling have met.

    Parent tips

    Slow is the whole trick — narrate what is happening in short steps and let your toddler watch you figure it out too. Confusion shared and solved teaches that not-knowing is a stop on the way, not a wall.

    Staying safe

    All feelings welcome — confusion included, no matter how small the trigger looks from up here. The honest note: confusion during big changes (moves, new siblings, new beds) deserves extra slowness and extra cuddles, not just a word.

    This lesson pairs with the Confused flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Emotions & Feelings (Toddler 7).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · EMOTIONS & FEELINGS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Bored — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson names the feeling that arrives on quiet afternoons: bored. The card gives the floppiness a face, and the lesson plants one small idea and stands back.

    What is this?

    Bored is the nothing-feels-interesting feeling — flopped body, distant stare, toys that were fine yesterday and are suddenly wrong. The card shows it honestly, as a feeling everyone gets.

    What does it mean?

    Boredom is the doorway to invented play: a toddler given one tiny idea at the bored moment usually spins it into twenty minutes. The feeling is uncomfortable on purpose — it is the mind asking for a job.

    What does the child need to know?

    Expect a flop, a whine, or bored said like a complaint — all answers, and the complaint is the invitation. Name the feeling, offer one seed, not a schedule, and let the growing be theirs.

    Why this matters

    Quiet hours arrive daily, and a toddler who owns the word for the lull can move through it faster. You are not the entertainment department — you are the seed merchant.

    What it teaches

    Imagination, self-directed play, and feeling vocabulary for the flat moods — the earliest independence training there is.

    Words to learn

    boredideaplaynewtoyshmm

    Say this to your child

    “"Bored. This face feels bored — nothing feels fun. Hmm! When you feel bored, tell me, and we will find one little idea. Look — two blocks… I wonder what they could be. Now it is your game."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card on a suitably floppy afternoon: bored — this face cannot find anything fun. Sympathise first; the feeling is real.
    2. Make the face together: droopy shoulders, hollow sigh, a bored ahh. The drama gets a laugh, which is already half a cure.
    3. Teach the move: when you feel bored, tell me — and we will find one new idea together. One idea, not ten.
    4. Plant the seed small: set two toys side by side, say one sentence — the dolly is hungry, I wonder — and walk a step away. The distance is deliberate.
    5. When the play catches, leave it alone. Come back later and name what grew: you were bored, and look what you invented! The arc is the lesson.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows an illustrated child having a bored feeling — one flat, floppy face. Ask your toddler to find the bored face, then to do their very best bored slouch beside it.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the bored face?" "Can you make a bored face?" "What could we do first?" "What did you invent?"

    What your child can say or do

    A floppy slump, a whined bored, or a shrug with eyebrows — the feeling arrives in body language first. A toddler who answers the seed with their own twist has already left the lesson behind, which is the goal.

    Out in the real world

    Flat afternoons come every week. Name the feeling, plant one idea, resist the rescue — and the empty stretch slowly turns into the birthplace of the best games.

    Try it together

    Two-toy spark: choose any two toys that rarely meet, set them side by side, and wonder out loud for exactly one sentence. Then be busy elsewhere; the spark catches best unwatched.

    Understanding check

    After the next floppy patch, ask how you felt before the game. Bored, a shrug, or a finger landing on the floppy face all pass. The longer pass mark: stretches of invented play growing quietly longer, week on week.

    Parent tips

    Name the feeling, plant the seed, then genuinely step back — boredom plus one idea is the recipe, boredom plus a show is the trap. You do not have to fill every flat minute; nobody could.

    Staying safe

    Bored toddlers go hunting, and their hunting grounds include stairs, cupboards and the bin: keep the floppy zones safe and doors latched. The honest note — a bored two-year-old left entirely alone finds trouble; nearby-but-busy is the sweet spot.

    This lesson pairs with the Bored flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Emotions & Feelings (Toddler 7).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · EMOTIONS & FEELINGS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Hurt — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson handles the feeling every toddler meets at ground level: hurt. The card gives the ouch a face, and the routine gives it an order — cuddle first, word second.

    What is this?

    Hurt is the ouch feeling — a stumble, a bonk, a pinch, arriving with tears before anyone can explain. The card shows a mild hurt face, safely framed, for studying after the fact.

    What does it mean?

    Comfort comes first because bodies shout louder than minds: a hurt child needs arms before vocabulary. Once the tears settle, the word hurt gives the memory a shape — and retold stumbles stop running the whole afternoon.

    What does the child need to know?

    Expect ouch delivered at volume, tears, or a point at the sore bit. The lesson is the order: comfort, settle, then name — this card joins in afterwards, never in the first seconds.

    Why this matters

    Stumbles are daily and mostly small. A standing routine — cuddle, calm, name, retell — turns each bonk from a drama into an event with a beginning and an end.

    What it teaches

    Feeling vocabulary for body signals, comfort-seeking and comfort-giving, and memory-shaping — small stories that make sense of small injuries.

    Words to learn

    hurtouchbumpcuddlekissbetter

    Say this to your child

    “"Hurt. This face has an ouch — see the tears? When you feel hurt, I come first, with cuddles. Then we say hurt together. Kiss it better, cuddle it better — and the hurt gets smaller and smaller."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card at a calm moment: hurt — this face has an ouch. See the tears? They are already drying. Keep it light.
    2. Practise the routine backwards, in play: kiss a teddy’s sore paw, wrap it in a cuddle, and say the words — hurt, cuddle, better. Your toddler will run this script for real.
    3. Say the order out loud: when you feel hurt, cuddles come first, and the word comes after. Both are coming; the arms are just faster.
    4. At the next real bonk: scoop, settle, comfort — no lesson yet. Once the sobs slow, name it softly: that hurt, did it not? Then let the kissing-the-better ritual finish the job.
    5. Retell it at tea: you fell, it hurt, you had a cuddle, and now — better! The story with the ending is what makes stumbles survivable memory.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows an illustrated child having a mild hurt feeling — one teary face with a small ouch. Ask your toddler to find the hurt face, then to give the card a gentle pat or a pretend kiss better.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the hurt face?" "What does the hurt face need?" "What comes first — cuddles or words?" "All better now?"

    What your child can say or do

    Ouch arrives years before hurt does — the sound is the honest first word. Expect tears in real moments, a pointing finger at the sore bit, and, on the card, a gentle pat or a blown kiss.

    Out in the real world

    Real bonks run the routine for you: scoop, comfort, wait, name, retell. The card comes out after, when the knee is forgotten — that is the moment the feeling becomes a word with a story attached.

    Try it together

    Teddy hospital: a soft toy with a sore paw, a cuddle, a pretend kiss, a bandage made of a sock. Your toddler as the comforter learns the routine from the giving side — which is how it becomes automatic.

    Understanding check

    After the next small injury, listen once it settles: ouch, hurt, or a point at the card mid-cuddle all pass. The deeper mark: your toddler bringing you the sore finger calmly, already knowing the order of events.

    Parent tips

    In the moment, comfort outranks teaching, always — the card is for afterwards. Keep the retelling short and kind: one fall, one cuddle, one better. Toddlers re-read these little stories more often than you think.

    Staying safe

    Cuddle first, assess second: check the bump properly once the tears slow — a real injury is grown-up work, not a kissing game, and help gets called when it looks beyond a cuddle. The card never substitutes for checking.

    This lesson pairs with the Hurt flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Emotions & Feelings (Toddler 7).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · EMOTIONS & FEELINGS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Loved — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson gives the deepest feeling its name: loved. The card pairs the word with the warmth, and the week makes sure the word arrives on ordinary days, not just special ones.

    What is this?

    Loved is the warm, safe, held feeling — cuddles, tucked blankets, being found in a crowd. Your toddler has lived it since day one; the card simply hands the feeling its word.

    What does it mean?

    Love named becomes love owned: a toddler who hears loved attached to cuddles and ordinary Tuesdays learns the feeling is permanent, not earned. That security is the platform every other feeling stands on.

    What does the child need to know?

    Expect a hug, a grin, or loved said as a happy mumble into your shoulder. There is nothing to test here — the lesson is the saying, and the saying is the lesson.

    Why this matters

    The word costs nothing and pays forever. Said at bedtime, after a storm, in the middle of nothing at all, it builds the constant your toddler will stand on for years.

    What it teaches

    Attachment language, security, and emotional vocabulary for the feeling under all feelings — the word that makes the rest of the deck safe to explore.

    Words to learn

    lovedlovehugcuddlekisswarm

    Say this to your child

    “"Loved. This face is feeling loved — warm and safe and snug. That is my heart about you! I love you at cuddle time, I love you after storms, I love you all day long. Come here — cuddle time."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card at cuddle time with your toddler already in your arms: loved — this face is feeling loved. Let the word land inside the hug.
    2. Connect word and warmth: this face shows loved — it is exactly how I feel about you. Say it slowly, once, and let the cuddle finish.
    3. Ask where the loved face is; a point from inside the hug is the perfect answer.
    4. Say loved at ordinary moments all week: after breakfast, after a storm, halfway through shoes. The word should feel like furniture, not a fireworks display.
    5. Let your toddler give it back: a hug offered to you or to teddy is loved spoken in their own language — receive it like the news it is.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows an illustrated child feeling loved — one warm, cosy face. Ask your toddler to find the loved face, then to give someone nearby a hug to match it.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the loved face?" "How does a cuddle feel?" "Who loves you?" "Who do you love?"

    What your child can say or do

    A hug that arrives as the answer, a loved said with milk still on the top lip, or a kiss blown at the card — the feeling barely needs the word. Expect to be hugged mid-sentence; accept it as fluency.

    Out in the real world

    Loved moments are everywhere already: the towel at bath time, the reunion at the gate, the last story. Attach the word to two a day and the feeling gets its name on the regular.

    Try it together

    Love-round game: at bedtime, name three people who love your toddler — one, two, three, each with a squeeze. The roll call turns love from a feeling into a list your toddler can hold.

    Understanding check

    There is no test for being loved — the pass mark is the cuddle itself. Watch instead for the word arriving in your toddler’s play: a teddy told it is loved means the vocabulary is moving in for good.

    Parent tips

    Say it on flat days as much as golden ones — loved needs to feel like a steady constant, never a reward for behaviour. The word after a meltdown teaches the deepest version: love that does not depend on the weather.

    Staying safe

    No safety angle here — this is the safest word in the deck. The honest note: keep it unconditional. Loved said at tantrums and triumphs alike is what makes the word load-bearing.

    This lesson pairs with the Loved flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Emotions & Feelings (Toddler 7).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · EMOTIONS & FEELINGS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Friendly — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson names the outward feeling: friendly, the hello-feeling that waves its whole arm. The card gives it a face mid-wave, and the games give it somewhere safe to practise.

    What is this?

    Friendly is the open, welcoming feeling — a wave, a smile, a hello offered to dogs, babies and postwomen alike. The card shows it in motion: one illustrated child, mid-wave.

    What does it mean?

    Friendliness is a feeling and a skill at once: the warmth arrives on its own, and the greeting — wave, hello, smile — is the part that improves with practice. Toys make a patient practice crowd.

    What does the child need to know?

    Expect a big arm wave, a hello or hi delivered to the card, or a wave aimed at the window. Greetings to strangers remain optional and adult-supervised — the practice happens at home first.

    Why this matters

    Greetings structure a toddler’s whole social day: arriving, leaving, meeting, waving bye. A named friendly feeling with a rehearsed wave turns each one into a small victory lap.

    What it teaches

    Social greeting skills, feeling vocabulary for the outgoing moods, and confidence in first moves — the emotional machinery of making friends.

    Words to learn

    friendlyhellowavehibyesmile

    Say this to your child

    “"Friendly! This face is waving hello — look at that big wave! Can you wave? Hello, hello! We wave hello, we wave bye-bye. Being friendly is saying hi in your own way — a wave is plenty."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and wave at it: friendly — this face is saying hello! Wave back at the card from your toddler’s hand if they need a start.
    2. Practise the wave in the mirror: big wave, small wave, wave with both arms. Hello can be whispered, shouted, or just waved.
    3. Run greetings on the toys: wave hello to teddy, wave bye-bye to the duck, say hi to the bus rumbling past. Six greets a day keeps the wave warm.
    4. At real arrivals, offer the choice: hello, wave, or just watch? Any of the three counts as friendly — the feeling is the point, the words are optional extras.
    5. Close the loop on goodbyes too: friendly has a second act — wave bye-bye, blow a kiss. Endings done warmly are half of friendliness.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows an illustrated child giving a friendly wave — one open face with a hand in the air. Ask your toddler to find the friendly face, then to wave back at it just as big.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the friendly face?" "Can you wave like that?" "Who shall we say hello to?" "Can you wave bye-bye?"

    What your child can say or do

    A full-arm wave with optional sound effects — ha! or hi! — is the complete answer. Some toddlers wave at everything for a day, including the fridge; the enthusiasm is the lesson taking hold.

    Out in the real world

    Greets happen all day at toddler height: the neighbour, the bus driver, the dog on the other side of the fence. Each wave is a repetition, and each one is free.

    Try it together

    Wave parade: march through the house greeting everything — hello chair, hello window, bye-bye bath. The parade makes greetings a game and the game makes the real ones easy.

    Understanding check

    At the next real arrival, watch for the wave — instant, delayed, or from behind your leg, all pass. A hello aimed at a teddy before the real person counts too; the practice crowd gets credit.

    Parent tips

    Let the child choose the volume and the timing of every hello — the feeling is theirs to spend. Your job is the warm example: wave first yourself, and let friendliness be caught rather than taught.

    Staying safe

    Real greetings happen on your terms: grown-ups decide who gets close, hands get held near roads, and waving from your hip is always a valid distance. Friendly and careful are the same lesson.

    This lesson pairs with the Friendly flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Emotions & Feelings (Toddler 7).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · EMOTIONS & FEELINGS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Kind — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson catches the quiet feeling with the biggest reputation: kind. The card shows a child being kind and helpful, and the week is full of small versions waiting to be named.

    What is this?

    Kind is the helping, gentle feeling — the soft pat, the shared bite, the blanket carried to a cold teddy. The card shows it in action: a child being kind and helpful.

    What does it mean?

    Kindness named gets repeated: a toddler who hears that was kind! while the gentle hands are still gentle learns exactly what the word points at. Named kindness is how a habit begins.

    What does the child need to know?

    Catch it small and in the moment: the pat, the crumb, the delivery of a shoe. Expect a grin, a kind repeated, or more gentleness on the spot — the behaviour blooms under attention.

    Why this matters

    Kindness happens hourly at two and almost never gets a headline. Naming it turns scattered gentle moments into a self-image: I am someone who is kind.

    What it teaches

    Prosocial behaviour, gentle-hands habits, and feeling vocabulary for the caring moods — the emotional start of ethics, built on teddy care.

    Words to learn

    kindgentlehelpsharesoftcare

    Say this to your child

    “"Kind! This child is being kind — gentle hands, helping. Can you do gentle hands? Stroke, stroke — soft. You gave Teddy a blanket — that was kind! Kind means helping and being gentle. You know how to do that."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and name the action inside the feeling: kind — this child is being kind and helpful. Look how gentle.
    2. Practise gentle hands right there: stroke your own arm, stroke your toddler’s arm, then let them stroke yours. Slow is the whole secret.
    3. Run it on the toys: teddy gets a blanket, dolly gets a pat, the rabbit gets a gentle touch. Say kind each time the hands stay soft.
    4. Catch the real thing and name it instantly: you gave Teddy your blanket — how kind! The naming must land while the moment is still warm.
    5. Let kindness be contagious: when your toddler is kind to you, say so, and accept it. The feeling needs to be received as much as practised.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows an illustrated child being kind and helpful — one caring face, one helping gesture. Ask your toddler to find the kind child, then to show you their own gentle hands.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the kind child?" "Can you do gentle hands?" "How did you help today?" "Was that kind or rough?"

    What your child can say or do

    A pat that slows down mid-air when the word lands, a kind echoed proudly, or a teddy wrapped without prompting — all are the word taking root. Rough moments are information too: gentle hands, said once, and try again.

    Out in the real world

    Kindness grows at home on real targets: the baby, the cat, the visitor, you. One named kind moment a day is the whole curriculum — and it compounds.

    Try it together

    Gentle-zoo: gather the soft toys and visit each one with careful strokes — kind hands for the lion, kind hands for the bear. The zoo runs on the same skill the family cat is hoping for.

    Understanding check

    Watch for gentleness arriving without prompting: a soft pat, a shared bite, a helped-up friend. Name each one. A toddler who says kind while doing it has closed the loop entirely.

    Parent tips

    Notice kindness rather than demanding it — the feeling grows on being caught, not commanded. Keep the bar low and the catches frequent: a single gentle pat is headline material at two.

    Staying safe

    Gentle hands have real destinations: pets get stroked on the back with permission, babies get supervised hellos, and grown-ups stay within reach of every new meeting. Kindness and safety practice the same hands.

    This lesson pairs with the Kind flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Emotions & Feelings (Toddler 7).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · EMOTIONS & FEELINGS · AGES 2 YEARS

    Brave — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    This lesson names the feeling your toddler produces daily without applause: brave. The card shows a child being brave by trying, and the lesson retells those moments as true stories with heroes.

    What is this?

    Brave is the wobbly-and-anyway feeling — the big slide attempted, the loud dryer endured, the new food tasted. The card shows it honestly: a child being brave by trying, not by winning.

    What does it mean?

    Brave is scared plus one step: the two feelings share a body, and the story that joins them — it was big, the wobble was real, and then you did it — is what teaches a toddler their own courage.

    What does the child need to know?

    Keep the word for genuine effort by your toddler’s own measure — their hard, not yours. Expect a grin, a brave repeated, or the deed done again immediately. All pass; the immediate repeat most of all.

    Why this matters

    Hard things arrive hourly at two, and each one is a story waiting for its ending. A named brave turns scattered trials into a self-image with a spine.

    What it teaches

    Confidence, effort vocabulary, and the fear-to-action arc — emotional storytelling that makes courage a habit instead of an accident.

    Words to learn

    bravetrybigstepscareddid

    Say this to your child

    “"Brave! This child is trying the big thing — see the brave face? Brave is feeling scared, and doing it anyway. You know what? You do that all the time! You are brave. Let us tell the story of when you did it."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card and tell its story: brave — this child is trying something big, even though it feels scary. Brave means scared, and doing it anyway.
    2. Make the face together: determined chin, deep breath, fists ready. The posture is half the feeling — borrow it freely.
    3. Catch it live at the next wobble-and-try: you felt scared, and you went down the slide anyway — brave! Say it while the landing is still bouncy.
    4. Retell the day’s brave moment at dinner as a three-beat story: the big thing, the scared feeling, the doing it anyway. Your toddler takes the hero role, truthfully.
    5. Keep real danger where it belongs: brave is for the child’s own hard things — grown-ups own roads, water and heights. Say the boundary once so the word stays safe to use.

    Look closer at the picture

    The card shows an illustrated child showing bravery by trying — one determined face mid-attempt. Ask your toddler to find the brave child, then to make their own brave face and take one big pretend step.

    Ask your child

    "Where is the brave child?" "Can you make a brave face?" "What big thing did you try today?" "What happened next?"

    What your child can say or do

    A determined march toward the thing, a brave whispered at the top of the slide, or the story retold with the hero’s part pointed at themselves — all are the word moving in. Wobbles still happen; brave includes them.

    Out in the real world

    Brave moments line up daily: the hand-dryer, the big step, the new babysitter. Catch one, tell it as a story, and the word starts doing quiet work in the background of every hard thing.

    Try it together

    Story-theatre: retell today’s brave moment with toys playing the parts — the slide, the wobble, the try. Your toddler directs, corrects and casts themselves as the hero, which is accurate casting.

    Understanding check

    At the next hard thing, listen afterwards: brave, did it, or a point at the card during the retelling all pass. Then watch for the second attempt happening sooner — courage compounding is the real report card.

    Parent tips

    Save the word for genuine effort by your toddler’s own measure — brave spent on easy things goes bankrupt fast. Tell the wobble part honestly: the scared bit is what makes the brave bit mean something.

    Staying safe

    Brave is for wobbles, not hazards: roads, water, fires and high places stay grown-up decisions, always and without negotiation. Say it plainly — you are brave, and I keep you safe — so both truths can hold hands.

    This lesson pairs with the Brave flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Emotions & Feelings (Toddler 7).
